content: The Korean Society of Thyroid-Head and Neck Surgery (KSTHNS) has developed comprehensive clinical practice guidelines specifically for the surgical management of laryngeal cancer. These guidelines were created by a multidisciplinary task force that conducted a systematic review of relevant literature from databases such as EMBASE, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and KoreaMed. The task force used search terms tailored to address key clinical questions, and evidence-based recommendations were formulated based on the findings. External expert reviews and Delphi questionnaires were employed to achieve consensus on these recommendations. The guidelines focus exclusively on surgical treatment for laryngeal cancer, assuming that surgery has been selected as the treatment modality following a multidisciplinary discussion. Non-surgical treatments, such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy, are not addressed. A total of 62 evidence-based recommendations were developed, categorized into 32 sections, to assist clinicians in managing patients with laryngeal cancer. These recommendations are also intended to guide counselors and health policymakers. Laryngeal cancer is the second most common head and neck cancer after thyroid cancer, with an incidence of approximately 7 per 100,000 individuals. Historically, total laryngectomy was the primary surgical treatment, but it often resulted in significant postoperative quality-of-life challenges due to the loss of voice. However, advancements in organ-preserving treatments, such as those introduced by the Veterans Affairs Administration and Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG 91-11), have shifted the standard of care toward non-surgical options. Despite this, surgery remains a critical treatment option, particularly for advanced T4 cases. Recent innovations, such as transoral surgery and supracricoid laryngectomy (SCL), have expanded surgical indications and improved functional and oncological outcomes, even in selected advanced cases. The guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based decision-making in the context of rapidly evolving treatment trends. They are not intended to replace clinical judgment but rather to serve as an adjunct to it. The target population includes patients with suspected or diagnosed laryngeal cancer who have agreed to undergo surgery after discussions about multimodal treatment options. The guidelines provide detailed recommendations for diagnostic workups, preoperative evaluations, initial surgical treatments for glottic and supraglottic carcinomas, postoperative follow-up, management of complications, and strategies for handling recurrences. The intended users of these guidelines are primarily head and neck surgeons treating laryngeal cancer patients. However, the detailed information provided is also valuable for other clinicians involved in multimodal treatment teams, including medical and radiation oncologists, rehabilitation specialists, nurses, counselors, and health policymakers. The task force was led by a chairman and included two secretaries and 12 members. A practice committee of 14 members was later organized to perform literature searches and reviews. The committee maintained editorial independence from KSTHNS. Key clinical questions were identified and categorized into four main areas: preoperative evaluation, surgery for glottic cancer, surgery for supraglottic cancer, and postoperative follow-up and management of complications and recurrences. A systematic literature search was conducted, and the quality of evidence was assessed using tools such as the Risk of Bias Assessment Tool for Nonrandomized Studies (RoBANS) and A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR). Recommendations were graded using the American College of Physicians (ACP) grading system, which classifies recommendations as either strong or weak based on the quality of evidence. Consensus on the recommendations was achieved through expert consultations and Delphi panels composed of experienced head and neck surgeons. The Delphi process involved two rounds of questionnaires, with response rates of 72% and 80%, respectively. Recommendations that failed to achieve consensus were removed from the final manuscript. The guidelines acknowledge certain limitations, including the reliance on expert opinions and retrospective case series due to the lack of high-quality studies. Additionally, the guidelines were developed with a focus on surgical treatment and should not be interpreted as favoring surgery over non-surgical options. The lack of sufficient Korea-specific data also limited the ability to make nation-specific recommendations, highlighting the need for multicenter studies to publish Korean treatment data. The guidelines will be published in an open-access journal to ensure broad accessibility and will be advertised on the KSTHNS homepage. Reprints will be distributed to otolaryngology clinics treating laryngeal cancer patients. The task force will remain active as a special committee within KSTHNS, and the guidelines will be revised and updated every 3 to 5 years to incorporate new clinical data and advances in surgical and diagnostic techniques. The guidelines emphasize that oncological outcomes of radiation therapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy are comparable to those of surgery, with the former often providing superior quality-of-life outcomes. However, surgery remains the preferred option for very advanced T4 cases. Patients should be provided with comprehensive information about all treatment modalities to make informed decisions. The guidelines assume that a thorough discussion of the pros and cons of surgical versus non-surgical strategies has been completed before surgery is chosen as the treatment modality.
